properties.description:
Polemoniaceae, Ericales.

I originally called this A. hutchinsifolia, but that the corollas of that species are glandular-puberulent abaxially. It's difficult for me to make a confident ID without basal leaves, but A. heterostyla is my best guess.

BMDO2021-NR-16

Cochrane gilia, Aliciella heterostyla, Monitor Range, Humboldt Toiyabe National Forest, Saulsbury Wash, Ralston Valley drainage, elevation 1805 m (5915 ft).  Also identifiable is capped cryptantha (Greeneocharis circumscissa).

This species is endemic to (but locally common in) northern Nye County, Nevada, at the southern edge of the Great Basin.  It is closely related to another Nevada endemic, Aliciella nyensis, found a little farther south.  Aliciella heterostyla was only recognized as distinct in 1994 based on its dimorphic flowers which enforce cross-pollination.

properties.description:
A bit under 5000’, easterly aspect. Growing in volcanic sands in the middle and sides of a two-track. Not as far along in senescence as some other Astragalus spp. nearby.

Leaflets almost leathery. Latin for “to stretch out”.

Not a ton of info on this species. Mozingo and Williams in ‘82 speculated that it may have been more widespread in the past. Range seems to loosely track old Lake Lahontan, though not the shorelines exclusively.

properties.description:
Steamboat monkeyflower, Diplacus ovatus, Nevada, Jobs Peak Ranch Trail, Carson Range, Sierra Nevada, Sheridan, Carson Valley drainage, elevation 1481 m (4860 ft).

Limited to the slopes and valley floors just east of the Sierra Nevada in western Nevada, from Reno south through Carson Valley, this species is found on various soil types, including decomposed granite such as here, at elevations between about 1400-1650 meters (4600-5400 feet).

Care must be used to distinguish this species from other members of the Diplacus nanus - Diplacus mephiticus group, especially toward the south end of its range.  Diplacus ovatus differs by its combination of exclusively magenta flowers; largest leaves ovate to obovate, >8 mm wide, at least some acuminate to cuspidate; most plant parts glandular-villous (not merely puberulent).

Steamboat monkeyflower, Diplacus ovatus, Nevada, Virginia Range, Geiger Grade, Steamboat Creek - Truckee Meadows drainage, elevation 1635 m (5360 ft).

Limited to the slopes and valley floors just east of the Sierra Nevada in western Nevada, this species is found on various soil types, including these severe altered andesite soils in the foothills surrounding the greater Reno-Sparks area of far western Nevada.  Deep hydrothermal alteration of these volcanic deposits left behind sulfide minerals, which slowly oxidize to sulfuric acid as they become exposed at the surface.  This creates patches of highly acidic (pH 3-4), brownish orange to white soils that are largely barren of vegetation.  Those few species that are able to tolerate these harsh soil conditions enjoy reduced competition from other vegetation.

Steamboat monkeyflower, Diplacus ovatus, Nevada, Sierra Nevada, Carson Range, Steamboat Creek - Truckee Meadows drainage, elevation 1405 m (4615 ft).

This rare species is endemic to various soils in the Geiger Grade and Steamboat Hot Springs area of southern Washoe County, Nevada, southward to Carson City and the Carson Valley of Douglas County.  Last year it was in mass bloom in many locations, including the siliceous sinter spring mound of Steamboat Hot Springs.  Care must be used to distinguish this species from other members of the Diplacus nanus - Diplacus mephiticus group, especially toward the south end of its range.  Here near the type locality the identity is more straightforward.

Steamboat Hot Springs included active geysers and spring mound deposition up until the late 1980s when above-ground activity ceased.  Although this was about the time that geothermal energy development started up near the site, prior regional groundwater drawdown in the south Reno area may have reduced the near-surface reservoir for geyser activity. Also visible in the image is the even rarer Steamboat buckwheat (Eriogonum ovalifolium var. williamsiae).

properties.description: Draba sphaeroides growing above the saddle between Prospect and Cougar Peaks, on the southeast ridge below Cougar Peak, Jarbidge Mountains, Elko County, Nevada. The cespitose growth habit, leaves not in tight rosettes and covered with stalked 2-4-rayed stellate hairs, scapes glabrate, flowers with yellow petals 3-4 mm long, developing fruits with styles about 1 mm long. Draba sphaeroides is endemic to Elko County, Nevada, in the Jarbidge, Ruby, and East Humboldt Mountains.

Returning to this population two weeks later, after the cows have been let back in to the area and see that multiple plants have been trampled. Many plants still flowering though. Some plants covered in the white silica pebbles and almost completely obscured save for their peduncle. Due to the matted form most plants seem to have escaped being munched on but the degradation of habitat is evident. Multiple plants covered in cow diarrhea. Ipomopsis tenuituba still somehow flowering, too, despite daytime temps at 100. Soil still moist 3 in down
The (incredibly small) documented population of this plant grew by a hundred yards or so this day.

properties.description:
10780’, growing in the crack of a granitic boulder. Really embracing that chasmophyte habit. Most flowers senescent, but there are a few hangers-on. This is the only guy I saw on the eastern side of the lake.

Are there plenty more up on the ridge? Yes. Was I expecting this one on a boulder right next to the lake? Absolutely not.

Subgenus Eucyla, and in the Eriogonum ochrocephalum complex.

Plant on the right with smaller leaves and flowering stems.  Specimen collected # Morefield 5761.

Eriogonum desertorum plant on the left in this observation: https://www.inaturalist.org/observations/85313550

This population appeared to be a fairly even mix of the two taxa, and still makes me somewhat hesitant about my identifications.

UPDATE September 2024: after reviewing my long buried specimens from this population, both forms clearly key to Eriogonum lewisii in Reveal's last major treatment, Intermountain Flora vol. 2A.  E. desertorum has even longer and narrower leaves than this.

properties.description:
altered andesite buckwheat, Eriogonum robustum, Nevada, Virginia Range, Geiger Grade, Steamboat Creek - Truckee Meadows drainage, elevation 1630 m (5350 ft).

This distinctive buckwheat is the signature rare species that is endemic to these peculiar "altered andesite" soils in the foothills surrounding the greater Reno-Sparks area of far western Nevada. Deep hydrothermal alteration of these volcanic deposits left behind sulfide minerals, which slowly oxidize to sulfuric acid as they become exposed at the surface. This creates patches of highly acidic (pH 3-4), brownish orange to white soils that are largely barren of vegetation. Those few species that evolve to tolerate these harsh soil conditions enjoy reduced competition from other vegetation, but in this case also become dependent on such conditions and don't survive anywhere else.
 
The same acidic soil conditions also allow a few species more common in the Sierra Nevada to survive on these isolated lower and drier desert sites.  This often includes sparse woodlands of Jeffrey pine (Pinus jeffreyi) and/or ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa) -- visible here in the background -- that rise above the surrounding matrix of sagebrush and pinyon-juniper vegetation.

In fact Eriogonum robustum is closely related to Eriogonum lobbii, a common higher-elevation species of the Sierra Nevada, of which it was once considered a variety.  (The two are fully distinct, however, with E. lobbii being a smaller species with prostrate stems and less branched flower heads.)  At one time long ago, maybe during a glacial maximum, ancestral populations of Eriogonum lobbii might have occupied both habitats, and then become isolated and diverged genetically on these sites as the post-glacial climate warmed and dried.

Uploaded from my Flickr site: https://www.flickr.com/photos/127605180@N04/

Tiehm buckwheat, Eriogonum tiehmii, Nevada, Esmeralda County, Silver Peak Range, Rhyolite Ridge, Fishlake Valley watershed, elevation 1846 m (6055 ft). Plant heavily excavated and fragmented in subpopulation 3 about 2 weeks after widespread damage to the Tiehm buckwheat population was discovered, and about 9 weeks after the initial signs of herbivore activity in the population. The preponderance of the photographic and other evidence continues to suggest that this damage was the result of an unusual mass-herbivory event, probably by Antelope Squirrels and maybe some Pocket Gophers. This was likely brought about by a "whiplash" in weather conditions in early summer of 2020 when, following several consecutive years of good to exceptional rainfall during which local rodent populations would have exploded, extreme heat and drought suddenly took hold in the southern Great Basin and persisted through fall of 2020 and well beyond. In the process of crashing back to drought levels, the rodent populations would have sought whatever moisture and nutrition remained available to them, which in Tiehm buckwheat habitat consisted mostly of the near-surface portions of the woody caudices and taproots of Tiehm buckwheat. The effectiveness of Tiehm buckwheat rootstocks as storage organs was demonstrated the following year, when the population showed unexpectedly high regeneration from damaged and even fully severed rootstocks, even as severe drought conditions persisted. But by then, the rodent populations had likely finished crashing to their new drought equilibria, and no further rodent damage was observed going through 2021. While such severe herbivory was not previously observed during the 35+ years Tiehm buckwheat had been known to science, "weather whiplash" events like this could unfortunately become more frequent as the total energy content of the atmosphere continues to increase going forward.

Tiehm buckwheat, Eriogonum tiehmii, Nevada, Esmeralda County, Silver Peak Range, Rhyolite Ridge, subpopulation 3, Fishlake Valley watershed, elevation 1841 m (6040 ft).

Regeneration under continued severe drought conditions in May 2021 of a large mat partially excavated and severely damaged during massive herbivory event that impacted the species in late 2020.

It turns out that the thick and extensive rootstocks of this species may be its "superpower," enabling it to store enough resources to support regeneration even under severe drought and/or damage conditions (assuming such conditions don't persist for too many years in a row). This may also explain why the near-surface portions of the rootstocks would have been attractive to local herbivore populations trying to survive under the drought and heat conditions in late 2020.

Ionactis caelestis is only known from a single population that occurs on the Aztec Sandstone near Bridge Mountain in the Spring Mountains of Clark County, Nevada (Nesom and Leary 1992).

Nesom and Leary (1992) estimated that there are about a thousand plants of the Ionactis spread over about 10 acres, and it is among the most abundant species in the area. While this species does not appear to be in danger of extinction, it certainly must be counted among the rarest in North America (Nesom and Leary 1992).

A couple other BLM botanists and myself surveyed for this species, and we believe we expanded the known range of this species slightly, but the known range is still confined to the Bridge Mountain area in Red Rock Canyon.

https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/2806841.pdf?seq=1

properties.description:
Grimes vetchling, Lathyrus grimesii, Nevada, Elko County, Independence Mountains, Independence Valley watershed, elevation 2441 m (8010 ft).

Specimen collected # Morefield 5619.
Grimes vetchling, Lathyrus grimesii, Nevada, Elko County, Independence Mountains, elevation 2347 m (7700 ft).

Grimes vetchling, Lathyrus grimesii, Nevada, Elko County, Independence Range, Dorsey Creek, Independence Valley watershed, elevation 2377 m (7800 ft).

This species is endemic to the Independence Range and adjacent Bull Run Mountains of Elko County.  It forms dense patches most easily surveyed in late summer after they have turned a distinctive brownish yellow.  Surveys were mainly by helicopter and on horseback.

From Kodachrome-64 color transparency film exposed with an Olympus OM-4T and Tamron 28-70mm zoom-macro lens. Scanned at 4000 dpi with a Nikon Coolscan 5000, and restored using Corel Paintshop Pro X4.

properties.description: pygmy poreleaf, Porophyllum pygmaeum, Nevada, Clark County, Desert National Wildlife Range, Sheep Range watershed, elevation 1355 m (4445 ft). These are some poor, rushed film photos of plants gathered for the type collection of this species. I first noticed this unnamed species tucked away on an herbarium sheet at Rancho Santa Ana Botanic Garden, soon after arriving there as a graduate student. Fellow student Aaron Liston (@aaronliston), Garden employee Sara Meury, and I made a first unsuccessful attempt to relocate the species in the general area noted on the specimen in May 1987. Visiting taxonomist Fritz Ehrendorfer and I made a second long trip for another attempt in early June. As seems to happen too often when so focused, we spent the whole day searching fruitlessly, until just before sunset and still 5 hours from home, when we finally located this large population. Thus the poor and rushed photos, restored as best I could from high resolution scans. The species is still only known from the west base and slopes of the Sheep Range on the Desert National Wildlife Range in Clark County, Nevada. Collection: Morefield 4511 & Ehrendorfer Publication: Keil, D.J. & J.D. Morefield. 1989. Porophyllum pygmaeum (Asteraceae), a distinctive new species from southern Nevada. Systematic Botany 14: 583-588.

In this rhyolite tuff gravel habitat, the stems stay mostly buried, which helps insulate them from heat and cold.  As the stems expand with water uptake, they temporarily shed some of the gravel, allowing more direct sun to reach their photosynthetic tissues.

altered andesite popcorn flower, Plagiobothrys glomeratus, Nevada, Virginia Range, Geiger Grade, Steamboat Creek - Truckee Meadows drainage, elevation 1630 m (5350 ft).

This humble annual Borage is one of a few rare plant species found on (and in this case limited to) these peculiar "altered andesite" soils in the foothills surrounding the greater Reno-Sparks area of far western Nevada.  Deep hydrothermal alteration of these volcanic deposits left behind sulfide minerals, which slowly oxidize to sulfuric acid as they become exposed at the surface.  This creates patches of highly acidic (pH 3-4), brownish orange to white soils that are largely barren of vegetation.  Those few species that evolve to tolerate these harsh soil conditions enjoy reduced competition from other vegetation, but also become dependent on such conditions and often (like this species) don't survive anywhere else.

The same acidic soil conditions also allow certain conifer species from the higher and wetter Sierra Nevada to the west to survive at these lower-elevation desert sites, so that these habitat patches are also noticeable by their sparse woodlands of Jeffrey pine (Pinus jeffreyi) and/or ponderosa pine (Pinus ponderosa) rising above the surrounding matrix of sagebrush and pinyon-juniper vegetation.

5200’, clay-loams. Area seems to be a semi-popular spot for OHV use.

Peavine Mountain

Rare NV endemic. Rosaceae, Rosales. Ivesia: named after botanist Eli Ives.

From genus on Peavine Mtn: leaves with 4-8(10) leaflets per side (not 20-35 per side).
Lots out, beautiful in flower!
Looks a lot like the webberi I saw on peavine, but not confident on that by any means.

properties.description:
Carson Valley monkeyflower, Erythranthe carsonensis, Nevada, Pine Nut Mountains, Hot Springs Mountain, Carson Valley drainage, elevation 1498 m (4915 ft).

Carson Valley monkeyflower was recognized as a distinct species by Naomi Fraga in 2012, after having been confused with Erythranthe (=Mimulus) montioides and E. rubellus since its discovery in the mid 1800s.  It is a rare plant species, known only from Washoe Valley, Eagle Valley, and Carson Valley of Carson City, Douglas County, and southern Washoe County Nevada, and small portions of adjacent Alpine County, California, and Lyon County, Nevada.  It has been found nowhere else in the western United States despite extensive searches.

The species grows mainly in sagebrush-bitterbrush vegetation on sandy soils of the valley bottoms and adjacent lower slopes, and has been significantly impacted by urban and residential development.  Favorable conditions in spring of 2016 and 2017 allowed for extensive surveys and discovery of large new populations.  Some of the new populations are on public lands well removed from immediate development, but the majority are still within or adjacent to ongoing urban and residential expansion.

Also visible in this image are rosy pussypaws (Calyptridium roseum).

Collection number Morefield 5861.

Uploaded from my Flickr site: https://www.flickr.com/photos/127605180@N04/

Altered tuff, shallow clayey soils. Individuals on lower slopes more robust; some measurements on leaves and involucres seem to kick this over to alexanderae, but geographically this is more in line with crosbyae.

Page 28 of the NV Vascular checklist would seem to indicate that this *could* still be considered alexanderae by some.

Subgenus Eucycla.

Update April 2026: we might be alexanderae after all.

properties.description: I almost can’t believe it myself, but it has to be this. We just went and saw Lewisia maguirei in the Quinn Canyon Range YESTERDAY. About 150 air miles from this location in the Spring Mountains. About 50 plants. South and west facing limestone slope near top of small ridge. We looked at the sepals of 20 flowers, 19 had 3 sepals and 1 had 4 sepals. Plants had 2-3 flowers per inflorescence. :)!

properties.description:
Las Vegas bearpoppy, Arctomecon californica, Nevada, Clark County, Black Mountains, Callville Wash - Lake Mead watershed, elevation 599 m (1965 ft).

Arctomecon californica does not occur in the present day state of California.  It was discovered in 1844 near present day Las Vegas which, at the time, was part of the Mexican Departamento de las Californias.

From 35mm Ektachrome Elite-100 color transparency film exposed with a Tamron 28-70 mm zoom-macro lens on an Olympus OM-4T body. Scanned at 4000 dpi with a Nikon Coolscan 5000, and restored using Corel Paintshop Pro X4.
